nodes.label: Dahia et al. (2005) studied a family with pheochromocytoma that had no known genetic defect. Multipoint parametric linkage analysis gave identical LOD scores of 2.97 for loci at chromosome 2cen and 16p13. A two-locus parametric linkage analysis gave a maximum LOD score of 5.16 under a double recessive multiplicative model, which the authors suggested meant both loci were required for the disease to develop.

Dahia et al. (2005) described a familial pheochromocytoma syndrome that they considered consistent with digenic inheritance. They concluded that it added a recessive digenic trait to the genetic heterogeneity of these tumors.

Dahia et al. (2005) detected allele-specific loss of heterozygosity (LOH) only at the chromosome 2 locus in all tumors from the family, which they considered consistent with a tumor suppressor gene. Transcription profiling identified 4 additional pheochromocytomas with a similar genetic pattern, which helped refine the chromosome 2 locus. High-density SNP-array LOH mapping found LOH within the chromosome 2 region in 18 of 62 pheochromocytomas, narrowing the locus to less than 2 cM.

Dahia et al. (2005) noted that pheochromocytomas result from mutations in at least 6 different genes, each part of a distinct autosomal dominant disorder, but that some families with pheochromocytoma have no known genetic defect. They concluded that their study provided evidence for 2 novel pheochromocytoma susceptibility loci.

Qin et al. (2010) had previously mapped a familial pheochromocytoma susceptibility locus (FP) to chromosome 2q11. Further affected relatives and additional linked families narrowed the locus to a 19.62-Mb region containing 205 genes.

Qin et al. (2010) found that the affected individuals in the original FP kindred showed a dominant pattern of transmission. Four mutation carriers in Family 1 had no clinical disease at ages 43 to 58 years, which suggests incomplete penetrance.

Qin et al. (2010) sequenced exons of genes in the FP locus using tumor DNA from the index case of Family 1. They identified a splice-site mutation in TMEM127, IVS3-2A>C (p.Leu138fs), predicted to produce a truncated 148-amino acid protein. The mutation was present in the germline and in all 6 other affected sibs, and absent from 2 unaffected sibs. The same mutation was found in a second, unrelated family (Family 5), and haplotype analysis excluded a common ancestor.

Qin et al. (2010) sequenced TMEM127 in 102 additional index pheochromocytoma cases (19 familial, 83 apparently sporadic) and found 6 additional mutations. Overall, 4 TMEM127 variants were found among 12 families without mutations in other susceptibility genes (about 30% of familial cases), and 3 were found among sporadic-appearing cases (about 3%). All mutations were germline, and none were present in 1,064 ethnically matched control alleles. Six of the 7 variants were splice-site or nonsense (truncating) mutations.

Qin et al. (2010) identified a heterozygous germline 1-bp insertion in TMEM127, c.150insA (p.Pro51fs), predicted to produce a 106-amino acid protein. The patient was adopted, so family history was unknown, and had a unilateral adrenal pheochromocytoma at age 25.

Qin et al. (2010) identified a heterozygous nonsense mutation in TMEM127, c.475C>T (p.Gln159X), in a family with 2 affected members (Family 3). Both had bilateral adrenal pheochromocytomas (4 tumors in total), with onset between ages 48 and 72.

Qin et al. (2010) identified a heterozygous 4-bp deletion in TMEM127, c.264-267delCAGA (p.Thr89fs), predicted to produce a 121-amino acid protein. The patient had no family history of pheochromocytoma and developed bilateral adrenal tumors at age 46.

Qin et al. (2010) identified a heterozygous splice-site mutation in TMEM127, IVS2-1G>T (p.Phe83fs), predicted to produce a 99-amino acid protein. The family (Family 6) had 2 affected members, both with bilateral adrenal pheochromocytoma and onset between ages 54 and 66.

Qin et al. (2010) identified a heterozygous missense mutation in TMEM127, c.268G>A (p.Val90Met), in a patient with no family history who had a unilateral adrenal pheochromocytoma at age 32. The affected residue is conserved among putative mammalian orthologs. Only germline DNA was available, so LOH could not be assessed.

Qin et al. (2010) reported a mean age at diagnosis of 45.3 years for pheochromocytoma in patients with TMEM127 mutations. This is similar to sporadic cases and older than syndromic cases. All tumors arose from the adrenal medulla, about half of patients had bilateral tumors, and no malignancy or recurrence was seen during 4 to 16 years of follow-up.

Qin et al. (2010) examined loss of heterozygosity (LOH) at the TMEM127 locus in 35 pheochromocytomas. All 19 TMEM127-mutant tumors tested showed LOH with loss of the wild-type allele, compared with 2 of 16 wild-type tumors, consistent with a 2-hit tumor suppressor mechanism. TMEM127 expression was 4-fold lower in mutant tumors, which the authors suggested reflected instability of the mutant transcript.

Qin et al. (2010) found that no protein product was detectable in HEK293 cells transfected with mutant TMEM127 constructs (M158 and M99), despite equivalent transfection efficiency. This supports a loss-of-function effect.

Qin et al. (2010) found by expression profiling that TMEM127-mutant pheochromocytomas clustered with NF1- and RET-mutant tumors and were enriched for kinase receptor signaling transcripts, not hypoxia transcripts. TMEM127-mutant tumors showed increased S6K phosphorylation compared with normal adrenal medulla and TMEM127 wild-type tumors.

Qin et al. (2010) found that TMEM127 knockdown increased phosphorylation of the mTORC1 targets 4EBP1 and S6K, increased cell size and increased proliferation. Overexpression of TMEM127 reduced mTORC1 signaling and proliferation, without affecting RAS activity or AKT phosphorylation. TMEM127 localized to the plasma membrane, early endosomes, Golgi and lysosomes, and colocalized with amino acid-activated perinuclear mTOR, suggesting that it is a compartment-specific negative regulator of mTORC1.

Yao et al. (2010) sequenced the TMEM127 gene in 990 individuals with pheochromocytoma and/or paraganglioma from 8 worldwide referral centers. The cohort included 898 previously unreported cases without mutations in other susceptibility genes. They identified 19 potentially pathogenic germline TMEM127 mutations in 20 independent families. A multiplex PCR-based method was used to screen 545 samples for large gene deletions, and none were found.

Yao et al. (2010) found that all TMEM127 mutation carriers had adrenal tumors. Seven had bilateral tumors (P = 2.7 x 10(-4)), and 5 of 20 had familial disease (P = .005). Median age at onset was 41.5 years in carriers and 45 years in patients without a mutation, which was not significantly different (P = .54). The most common presentation was a single benign adrenal tumor in a patient older than 40 years, and malignancy occurred in 1 carrier (5%). The authors concluded that germline TMEM127 mutations were associated with pheochromocytoma but not paraganglioma, and that they occurred in an age group often excluded from genetic screening algorithms.

Yao et al. (2010) expressed 5 novel TMEM127 mutants in cell lines and used confocal microscopy to compare them with wild type. The mutant proteins were diffusely localized, whereas wild-type TMEM127 showed a discrete multiorganelle distribution. The authors concluded that disease-associated mutations disrupt the intracellular distribution of the protein.

Takeichi et al. (2012) sequenced TMEM127 in germline DNA from 74 unrelated Japanese patients with pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma who were negative for mutations and deletions in RET, VHL, SDHB and SDHD. They found the same heterozygous germline 4-bp deletion (c.116_119delTGTC; p.Ile41ArgfsX39) in 2 unrelated patients (2.7%) with bilateral adrenal pheochromocytoma. Tumor DNA showed loss of heterozygosity from a 2q deletion. The deletion had been reported before in a Brazilian patient and was not found in 114 healthy ethnically matched controls.

Takeichi et al. (2012) found that the germline TMEM127 deletion occurred together with loss of heterozygosity from a 2q deletion in tumor DNA. They noted that this fits TMEM127 acting as a tumor suppressor gene.

Takeichi et al. (2012) presented their study as the first report of a pathologic role for TMEM127 mutation in pheochromocytoma in an Asian population. They found TMEM127 mutations in 2.7% of Japanese patients who were negative for RET, VHL, SDHB and SDHD mutations. They concluded that the prevalence and phenotype appeared similar to those in earlier studies.

Toledo et al. (2015) offered clinical and genetic screening to 151 individuals from a six-generation family that carried a germline TMEM127 mutation. Of 34 mutation carriers with clinical data, followed for 8.7 +/- 8.1 years, 11 (32%) were diagnosed with pheochromocytoma at a median age of 43 years. In 9 patients symptoms began at 29 years (range, 10-55 years), and 2 patients were asymptomatic. Tumors were multicentric in 5 patients (45%) and bilateral in 5 (45%). Six patients (54%) had at least one adrenomedullary nodule smaller than 10 mm. No paragangliomas, distant metastases, or other manifestations were found.
Toledo et al. (2015) found that 47 members of a six-generation family with pheochromocytoma carried the germline TMEM127 c.410-2A>C mutation, which affects a splice site.

In this family, Toledo et al. (2015) estimated that the cumulative penetrance of pheochromocytoma in TMEM127 mutation carriers was 0% at ages 0-20 years, 3% at 21-30 years, 15% at 31-40 years, 24% at 41-50 years, and 32% at 51-65 years. The youngest patient was diagnosed at age 22 years, and the earliest symptoms were reported at age 10.

Toledo et al. (2015) described tumor multicentricity, nodular adrenomedullary hyperplasia, and symptom onset more than a decade before diagnosis as novel findings in TMEM127-related pheochromocytoma. They recommended offering TMEM127 genetic testing to at-risk individuals at age 22 years and annual clinical surveillance for mutation carriers.

Bausch et al. (2017) studied 972 unrelated registrants of the European-American-Asian Pheochromocytoma-Paraganglioma Registry who had no mutations in the classic pheochromocytoma- and paraganglioma-associated genes. Of these, 58 (6.0%) carried germline mutations in newer susceptibility genes: 29 in SDHA, 20 in TMEM127, 8 in MAX, and 1 in SDHAF2. Fifty-three of the 58 patients (91%) had familial, multiple, extra-adrenal, and/or malignant tumors and/or were younger than 40 years.

Bausch et al. (2017) found 7 malignant pheochromocytomas/paragangliomas among 63 tumors (11%) in patients with SDHA or TMEM127 mutations. Extra-adrenal tumors occurred in 28 mutation carriers (48%), including 23 of 29 SDHA carriers (79%), particularly as head and neck paragangliomas. SDHA-related disease began as early as 8 years of age. MAX-related tumors occurred almost exclusively in the adrenal glands and were frequently bilateral.

Bausch et al. (2017) estimated the penetrance of SDHA mutations at 39% by age 40 years. Penetrance differed significantly between index patients (45%) and mutation-carrying relatives (13%; P less than 0.001).

Bausch et al. (2017) recommended genetic testing for SDHA, TMEM127, MAX, and SDHAF2 in patients at high clinical risk whose classic susceptibility genes are mutation negative. They also recommended regular, systematic whole-body investigation for gene-specific prevention and early detection.

Stütz et al. (2020) reported a 61-year-old woman with a 4 x 4 x 6 cm paraganglioma in the left supraclavicular fossa. It showed MIBG uptake, plasma free metanephrines were normal, and histology was positive for synaptophysin and chromogranin. She also had acromegaly from a 13-mm GH-secreting pituitary macroadenoma. She had paroxysmal hypertensive crises, which the authors attributed to the acromegaly, and multinodular goiter; her family history was unremarkable. Both tumors were cured by surgery, and she remained well after 10 years of follow-up.

In this patient, next-generation sequencing of PPGL susceptibility genes found a heterozygous intronic TMEM127 variant, c.245-10C>G in intron 2. It is absent from gnomAD and was classified as a variant of uncertain significance under ACMG criteria. Segregation could not be studied: her parents were deceased and her children declined testing. Because the variant lies between other known variants at c.245-7 and c.245-12, the authors suggested that it might disrupt the consensus splice site, but they noted that experimental confirmation was needed.

Armaiz-Pena et al. (2021) studied 110 index patients carrying germline TMEM127 variants. The data came from a registry, published reports and public databases. Mean age was 45 years (range, 21-84 years), and females outnumbered males (76 vs 34, P < .001). Most patients had pheochromocytoma (94; 85.5%). Paraganglioma (10; 9%) and renal cell carcinoma (6; 5.4%) also occurred, either alone or together with pheochromocytoma. One-third of patients had multiple tumors, 15.4% had a known family history, and metastatic disease was rare (2.8%).

Armaiz-Pena et al. (2021) reported that 82% of the catecholamine profiles of pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas in TMEM127 variant carriers involved epinephrine, either alone or combined with norepinephrine.

Armaiz-Pena et al. (2021) found that most TMEM127 variants (n = 63) occurred only once and 13 were recurrent (2-12 times). Truncating variants were more common overall. Nontruncating variants, however, predominated in presentations other than pheochromocytoma alone (36% in pheochromocytoma-only vs 69% in other presentations, P < .001). They also clustered disproportionately within the transmembrane regions (P < .01). Combining clinical and earlier experimental data, the authors proposed sorting variants into 4 groups by mutation type, location and predicted disruption.

Armaiz-Pena et al. (2021) concluded that patients with TMEM127 variants often resemble those with sporadic nonmetastatic pheochromocytoma. Paraganglioma and renal cell carcinoma may also occur, although the authors stated that the causal link requires further evaluation.

Delgado et al. (2022) reported a 65-year-old woman with hypertension, bilateral adrenal nodules on CT scan, and elevated urinary metanephrines, consistent with bilateral pheochromocytoma. She underwent laparoscopic bilateral adrenalectomy, and no recurrence was recorded after 5 years of follow-up.
In a 65-year-old woman with bilateral pheochromocytoma, Delgado et al. (2022) identified a mutation in the TMEM127 gene, c.117_120delGTCT, by genetic testing.
